 1             III.    SPS’S RESOURCE PLANNING PROCESS AND
 2                              EVALUATION METHODS

 3   Q.   Please generally describe SPS’s resource planning process.

 4   A.   In its simplest form, electric resource planning uses customer electric demand and

 5        energy forecasts to determine the appropriate sources of electric supply that should

 6        be developed to meet customer requirements in a reliable and cost-effective

 7        manner. In conducting resource planning, SPS compares its existing generating

 8        resources, including owned generating capacity and purchased power, to its

 9        projected annual peak firm load obligation over the planning period. Minimum

10        planning reserve margins are included to determine SPS’s capacity position. I

11        discuss SPS’s capacity position in more detail in Section IV of my direct testimony.

12   Q.   Please describe Southwest Power Pool’s planning reserve margin (“PRM”)

13        requirement.

14   A.   To provide reliable service, all electric utilities must have a minimum level of

15        capacity that exceeds the projected peak load to allow for system contingencies,

16        including generating unit or transmission outages and other uncertainties. The

17        available capacity in excess of the projected peak load is referred to as the “planning

18        reserve margin.” PRM requirements are frequently specified by the group of

19        interconnected utilities to which the utility belongs. SPS is a member of Southwest

                                                6
                               Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                 Direct Testimony
                                         of
                                  Justin L. Gable

 1   Power Pool and on July 18, 2025, Southwest Power Pool received approval of its

 2   consolidated filings ER24-1317 and ER24-2953 at the Federal Energy Regulatory

 3   Commission (“FERC”). These approvals allow Southwest Power Pool to adopt new

 4   accreditation methodologies and updates the way Southwest Power Pool will

 5   account for how different resource types, whether a wind generator, natural gas

 6   plant or other generating resource, can be counted on to reliably contribute to meet

 7   the regional demand for electricity, especially during times of greatest need.

 8   Southwest Power Pool uses two different approaches for its PRM requirement:

 9   Installed Capacity (“ICAP”) and Accredited Capacity (“ACAP”). Both are

10   designed to meet a 1-in-10-day reliability standard, meaning the system aims to

11   avoid a loss-of-load event more than once every ten years, on average. The primary

12   difference between them lies in how thermal generating units are counted towards

13   resource adequacy. For renewable resources and battery energy storage systems

14   (“BESS”), Southwest Power Pool uses the Effective Load Carrying Capability

15   methodology to determine their accredited capacity under both ICAP and ACAP.

16          However, when it comes to thermal resources:

17      •   Under the ICAP approach, thermal resources are accredited based on their

18          net dependable capacity (their maximum sustained output). The PRM under


                                          7
                                Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                  Direct Testimony
                                          of
                                   Justin L. Gable

 1          the ICAP approach implicitly incorporates the anticipated outages of these

 2          thermal units into the overall reserve percentage.

 3      •   Under the ACAP approach, the accredited capacity of thermal resources is

 4          reduced based on their historical performance, as measured by PBA. This

 5          means that actual historical availability and forced outages directly reduce

 6          the accredited value of thermal units. As a result, the PRM percentage

 7          required under the ACAP approach is lower than under the ICAP approach,

 8          because the reduced availability is already accounted for in the capacity

 9          value itself.

10          While Southwest Power Pool’s Open Access Transmission Tarriff

11   (“OATT”) incorporates both ICAP and ACAP approaches, the ACAP approach is

12   primarily used to determine resource adequacy. However, because the ICAP

13   approach offers a more relevant comparison to recent Southwest Power Pool

14   practices, I will also describe it below.

1    Q.   Please describe Southwest Power Pool’s Installed Capacity Planning Reserve

2         Margin, (“ICAP PRM”) Requirement.

3    A.   In July 2024, Southwest Power Pool Regional State Committee and Board of

4         Directors significantly updated their ICAP PRM requirements. Starting in summer

5         2026, the summer PRM will be 16%, and for winter 2026/27, the winter PRM will

6         be 36%. This higher winter PRM was in part driven by recent extreme winter

7         events, including Winter Storm Uri. This is also a notable change because it is the

 8        first time Southwest Power Pool has set a separate winter ICAP PRM.

 9               Looking ahead, recent Southwest Power Pool studies support further

10        increases to the ICAP PRM in 2029. These study results project the summer PRM

11        to rise from 16% to 17% and the winter PRM to increase from 36% to 38%.

12   Q.   Please describe SPS’s ACAP PRM Requirement.

13   A.   Southwest Power Pool provides each Load Responsible Entity (“LRE”) with its

14        specific ACAP PRM requirement for the initial implementation seasons and not

15        beyond. For SPS, these values were 7.06% for the Summer 2026 season and

16        14.52% for the Winter 2026/2027 season.

                                       Justin L. Gable

 1   Q.   What process does SPS use to assess its electric resource needs to serve

 2        customer load?

 3   A.   SPS’s resource need assessment is guided by the regulatory framework found in

 4        17.7.3 NMAC concerning the development of integrated resource plans for public

 5        utilities. This framework ensures the identification of “…the most cost-effective

 6        portfolio of resources to supply the energy needs of customers.” SPS’s assessment

 7        of electric resource needs includes determining both the magnitude of need as well

 8        as the type of resources needed. Additionally, resource need assessment must,

 9        depending on the jurisdiction, be conducted in accordance with regulatory

10        requirements specifying resource assessment processes and resource-specific

11        acquisitions (e.g., requirements for integrated resource planning and the number of

12        renewable resources in a supply portfolio).

13               SPS determines the types of resources that its electric supply system needs

14        by evaluating how different resource technologies integrate with SPS’s existing

15        electric supply to serve the overall system capacity and energy needs in a reliable

16        and least-cost manner. Typical solutions for meeting resource needs consist of the

17        following: enhancing current resources, demand management, acquiring new

18        resources, and conducting competitive bid solicitations for new long-term or short-

19        term energy and capacity. The ultimate decision is made based on the reliability
                                            10
                                         Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                           Direct Testimony
                                                   of
                                            Justin L. Gable

 1           and economic value of the alternatives, the risks inherent in each alternative, the

 2           ability to install the generation in a timely manner, and other factors affecting the

 3           project’s value to SPS and its customers. SPS has utilized computer software in its

 4           resource planning modeling processes for decades and currently uses EnCompass 2

 5           in its evaluation of the economic value of resource alternatives.

 6   Q.      What is EnCompass?

 7   A.      EnCompass is a production costing model that uses an algorithm to determine the

 8           most cost-effective portfolio of resources for a utility system from a prescribed set

 9           of resource technologies under given sets of constraints and assumptions. The

10           EnCompass model includes: (1) a modern “solve anything” algorithm; (2) hourly

11           operation detail; and (3) enhanced storage logic and ancillary services. The model

12           is also able to perform utility capital accounting (i.e., revenue requirement

13           calculations).

14                   In addition to the usual input variables required for a production costing

15           model, EnCompass incorporates a wide variety of resource expansion planning

16           parameters to develop a coordinated, integrated plan that best suits the utility



             2
                 EnCompass is owned by Yes Energy. Xcel Energy has a licensing agreement with Yes Energy
     for use of the model.
                                                     11
                                        Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                          Direct Testimony
                                                  of
                                           Justin L. Gable

 1        system being analyzed. For example, EnCompass incorporates resource expansion

 2        planning parameters such as alternative generation technologies available to meet

 3        future needs; renewable energy resources; unit capacity sizes; heat rates; load

 4        management; conservation programs; reliability limits; emissions trading; and

 5        environmental compliance options.

 6   Q.   Please describe the costs that SPS incorporates into the EnCompass model.

 7   A.   The EnCompass model includes the critical generation costs SPS incurs to provide

 8        electric service to its customers. The following list summarizes the costs that are

 9        typically included in the EnCompass model.

10              1. Fuel & Variable O&M 3

11                      •   Fuel costs for all electric power supply resources (owned and
12                          purchased) and market energy costs.
13                      •   Variable operation and maintenance (“VOM”) costs for existing and
14                          new generation facilities added to meet future need.
15                      •   Energy costs for new generation facilities added to meet future
16                          needs.

17              2. Costs of Purchased Power

18                      •   Purchased energy costs for all electric power supply resources.
19                      •   Capacity costs of purchased power.
20                      •   VOM costs of purchased power.

              Operation and maintenance.

 6             4. Transmission Costs

 7                   •   Electric transmission interconnection and network upgrade costs for

12   Q.   What are some of the major assumptions that influence EnCompass’s

13        evaluation of the most reliable and cost-effective portfolio of resources?

14   A.   The major assumptions influencing the EnCompass evaluation include:

15        1)    Natural Gas Price Forecast: The price of natural gas is an important variable.
16              SPS uses a combination of market prices and fundamental price forecasts,
17              based on multiple highly respected, industry leading sources, to calculate
18              monthly delivered gas prices. As the foundation of the gas price forecast,
19              Henry Hub natural gas prices are developed using a blend of market
20              information (New York Mercantile Exchange (“NYMEX”) futures prices)
21              and long-term fundamentally based forecasts from Wood Mackenzie and
22              S&P Global. The forecast is fully market-based for the first few years, then
23              transitions into blending the three sources to develop a composite forecast.
24              The Henry Hub forecast is adjusted for regional basis differentials and
25              specific delivery costs for each generating unit to develop final model inputs.
26              The weightings for each component at various time intervals of the forecast
27              period are shown in Table JLG-1 below.

 1               Table JLG- 1: Natural Gas Forecast Weightings

                    Months              NYMEX         S&P Global     Wood MacKenzie

            Current Year + 2 Years       100.0%          0.0%               0.0%


                  Thereafter              25%            37.5%             37.5%


 2   (2)   Coal Price Forecast – Coal price forecasts are developed using two major
 3         inputs: (1) current coal contract volumes and prices combined with (2) current
 4         estimates of required spot market coal volumes and prices. Typically, coal
 5         volumes and prices are under contract on a plant-by-plant basis for a one- to
 6         five-year term with annual spot volumes filling the remainder of the estimated
 7         fuel requirements of the coal plant. The spot coal price forecasts are
 8         developed by averaging price forecasts provided by multiple industry-leading
 9         consulting firms, as well as price indicators from recent request for proposal
10         responses for coal supply.

11   (3)   Market Electricity Prices – In addition to resources that exist within SPS’s
12         service territory, SPS has access to a regional market located outside its
13         service territory. SPS is a member of Southwest Power Pool, which operates
14         as a consolidated balancing authority and dispatches all available generation
15         resources within its boundaries. This consolidated dispatch allows SPS
16         access to energy resources outside of SPS’s service territory for purchases, as
17         well as the opportunity to sell from its generation sources to other market
18         participants.

19         SPS uses a simple average of long-term on-peak and off-peak electric energy
20         prices forecasts provided by Wood Mackenzie and S&P Global as the basis
21         for prices for assumed purchases from Southwest Power Pool South Hub.

22   (4)   Demand and Energy Forecast – Projections of future energy sales and
23         coincident peak demand are fundamental inputs into SPS’s resource need
24         assessment. SPS forecasts retail energy sales and customers by rate class for

                                      Direct Testimony

 1             each jurisdiction. Retail coincident peak demand is forecasted in the
 2             aggregate at the total SPS level. The wholesale energy sales and coincident
 3             peak demand forecasts are developed at the individual customer level of
 4             detail. SPS models its forecasts on a monthly basis and uses monthly
 5             historical data to develop the customer, energy sales, and coincident peak
 6             demand forecasts. Annual energy sales are an aggregation of the monthly
 7             energy sales estimates. Energy sales are forecasted at the delivery point and
 8             peak demand is forecasted at the generating source.

 9   Q.   Regarding Table JLG-1 above, why does SPS rely entirely on NYMEX for its

10        near-term natural gas pricing forecast?

11   A.   The first three years of the natural gas market as reflected by NYMEX are relatively

12        liquid and actively quoted in the marketplace. Thus, NYMEX accurately reflects

13        the near-term market outlook for natural gas prices. SPS relies on market prices in

14        the near-term portion of the forecast to reflect current market conditions.

15   Q.   After the first three years, why does SPS rely on a blend of fundamental

16        natural gas forecasts for the long-term natural gas forecast?

17   A.   Absent robust (and heavily traded) market trade data, it is reasonable to rely on

18        fundamental natural gas price forecasts that consider projected changes in supply

19        and demand conditions for long-term natural gas forecasts. SPS uses a blend of the

20        fundamental natural gas forecasts to capture multiple fundamental views in the

21        forecasting process and to mitigate the impact of relying too heavily on a single

22        forecast.

                                        Justin L. Gable

1    Q.   How does SPS incorporate system reliability into the Encompass model?

2    A.   As I describe above, SPS incorporates the company’s demand and energy

3         requirements in the EnCompass model—both of which are critical factors for

4         maintaining system reliability. To ensure SPS can meet its forecasted peak system

5         demand requirements, EnCompass requires sufficient resources to meet SPS’s

6         minimum planning reserve margin requirement. If SPS does not have enough

7         resources to meet the projected demand and planning reserve margin requirements,

 8        during expansion modeling, EnCompass will select additional resources. It is

 9        worth noting that the planning reserve margin is not a target and EnCompass may

10        select additional resources in excess of the planning reserve margin requirement to

11        create the cost-effective portfolio of resources.

12               When calculating the most cost-effective portfolio of resources,

13        EnCompass also considers the resources needed to meet SPS’s energy requirements

14        at all hours. For example, adding only solar generation may satisfy SPS’s summer

15        planning reserve margin requirement, but may result in SPS being energy deficient

16        when solar resources are not generating (most obviously in the nighttime hours).

17        EnCompass ensures the most cost-effective portfolio provides sufficient diversity

18        of resources to meet SPS’s expected energy needs at all times.


                                                16
                                     Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                       Direct Testimony
                                               of
                                        Justin L. Gable

 1   Q.   Does SPS incorporate other system reliability concerns in its decision making?

 2   A.   Yes. There are other factors that SPS must consider in its decision making. These

 3        factors can be incorporated in the EnCompass model or are evaluated externally.

 4        For example, based on guidance from subject matter experts, to ensure transmission

 5        stability, SPS has previously incorporated the cost of installing synchronous

 6        condensers into the EnCompass model. In addition, production cost models such

 7        as EnCompass benefit from perfect foresight, meaning the model knows how much

 8        energy will be available and needed in each hour. In reality, system operators do

 9        not have this luxury and often respond to unforeseen circumstances (e.g., weather

10        related events, transmission outages, etc.). The capability of a resource portfolio to

11        respond to unforeseen circumstances is an example of an external consideration to

12        the EnCompass model.

 1                       IV.    SPS’S GENERATING CAPACITY

 2   Q.   What will you discuss in this section of your testimony?

 3   A.   In this section, I will discuss SPS’s total system generating capacity position in

 4        relation to SPS’s demand and energy planning forecasts and Southwest Power

 5        Pool’s PRM requirements.

 6   Q.   How does SPS prepare its demand energy forecast?

 7   A.   SPS primarily uses regression modeling to forecast load. This statistical technique

 8        identifies and quantifies the relationship between historical electricity sales and a

 9        set of independent variables, such as economic indicators, demographic trends,

10        electricity prices, and weather patterns. Once this relationship is established, SPS

11        projects future demand by applying the model to forecasted values of those

12        independent variables. This data-driven and dynamic approach ensures the forecast

13        accurately reflects both historical trends and anticipated future conditions. SPS

14        Witness John M. Goodenough describes SPS’s demand and energy forecast in more

15        detail in his Direct Testimony.




                                               18
                                   Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                     Direct Testimony
                                             of
                                      Justin L. Gable

 1   Q.   What amount of additional capacity is required on SPS’s system to meet the

 2        increased minimum Summer PRM?

 3   A.   Beginning in Summer 2026, Southwest Power Pool’s minimum Summer PRM

 4        increases from 15% to 16% on an ICAP basis. On an ACAP basis, the Summer

 5        PRM is 7.06%. Although this number appears to represent a lower PRM, taken in

 6        conjunction with Southwest Power Pool’s new accreditation methodology, PBA for

 7        thermal resources and ELCC for intermittent and storage resources, the 1% increase

 8        in Summer 2026 represents an approximate 46 MW of additional need spread

 9        between PBA impacts and PRM impacts as compared to what a 15% PRM

10        requirement would have required.

11   Q.   Can you discuss the PBA and PRM requirements in the winter season?

12   A.   Southwest Power Pool has recognized the increasing risk of winter reliability

13        events. In response, Southwest Power Pool has implemented a distinct and more

14        stringent PRM requirement for the winter season. Historically, PRMs were

15        primarily focused on summer peak conditions. However, recent extreme weather

16        events have demonstrated the need for robust winter planning. For the 2025/2026

17        planning year, Southwest Power Pool has established a winter PRM of 15% on an

18        ICAP basis. This requirement escalates to 36% in 2026/2027 and projected to be


                                              19
                                    Case No. 25-00____-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                       Justin L. Gable

 1        38% by 2029/2030. While these values are expressed in ICAP terms, Annually,

 2        these values will be converted to an ACAP basis by Southwest Power Pool. PBA

 3        represents a significant shift in how capacity is valued. Rather than relying solely

 4        on a capacity value based on periodic testing, PBA adjusts each resource’s

 5        contribution based on its historical performance, particularly during peak demand

 6        periods. For thermal resources, this includes EFORd for both Winter and Summer

 7        seasons and EFOF for only Winter seasons. SPS has proactively integrated these

 8        requirements into its resource planning framework. In comparing the Winter PRM

8    Q.   What would be the amount of the deficiency payment?

9    A.   The deficiency payment calculation is defined in the Southwest Power Pool OATT

10        Attachment AA Section 14.2. Because the seasonal deficiency SPS is identifying

11        falls within two years of a change in the PRM requirement (15% for Winter 2025/26

12        to 36% for Winter 2026/2027), SPS would be subject to the Deficiency Payment

13        based upon the Sufficiency Valuation Curve found in SPP’s Business Practice

14        8300. However, this methodology depends on results of calculations performed by

15        SPP after the given season to calculate a Net Cost of New Entry (“Net CONE”) and

16        the Regional-wide resource adequacy position of the given season. At this time,

 5        represent a possible scenario where SPP’s total regional capacity continues to

 9                  = (77.484 MW * 1,000 kW/MW) * $85.61/kW-yr * 1.5
